readings.title: An evacuation map for a riverside street
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents beside a river received an evacuation map. Many assumed the nearest bridge was the safest route during a flood warning. The main obstacle was a map that did not explain bridge closure. The printed arrows crossed a low bridge that could close before nearby streets flooded. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a route walk with emergency staff. The group checked which paths remained passable under the warning conditions used in local plans. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated the highest route began farther from the bridge. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised map with a clearly named uphill meeting point. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: an emergency route must match the likely hazard. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in an evacuation map for a riverside street, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Keeping a neighbourhood contact tree current
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A neighbourhood association planned to call vulnerable residents during severe weather. Its contact list had not been updated for two years. The main obstacle was telephone details that no longer worked. Several volunteers had moved, and some residents did not want their numbers shared widely. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a consent-based contact review. Coordinators checked numbers privately and asked each person how they preferred to receive an alert. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated a smaller accurate list was more useful. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced regular updates with limited access to contact details. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: preparedness depends on trust as well as records. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in keeping a neighbourhood contact tree current, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A supply box in a shared building
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An apartment block placed emergency supplies near its entrance. Residents later found that batteries and bottled water had expired. The main obstacle was supplies without an inspection schedule. Everyone expected someone else to check the box after it was first installed. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used an inventory and expiry-date review. The building manager listed contents and asked residents which items local guidance actually recommended. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated routine maintenance mattered more than box size. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a dated checklist with named responsibility. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: an emergency resource must be ready when needed. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a supply box in a shared building, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Practising a storm warning message
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A school sent families a sample storm warning. Parents understood that lessons might stop but did not know how children would be collected. The main obstacle was a warning without practical collection steps. The message named the danger but left transport and contact arrangements unclear. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a short communication exercise. Staff asked families to describe what they would do after reading the message once. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated families needed a clear next action. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a staged alert with collection locations and timing. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: warnings are useful when they guide decisions. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in practising a storm warning message, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning community emergency preparation often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the neighbourhood emergency preparation programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关社区应急准备的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the emergency planning group proposing a small improvement to the neighbourhood emergency preparation programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the neighbourhood emergency preparation programme. People have noticed a map that did not explain bridge closure, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
